issues.failure_explanation: Lie-algebra equations determine equivariance only on the identity component. For the linear Lie group G={±1}, the Lie algebra is zero, so the proposed infinitesimal matrix imposes no constraints; nevertheless, the odd function x is not equivariant for the trivial output representation. The formal construction assumes connectedness, and the special parity treatment of O(3) does not establish the advertised arbitrary-group result.

failure_location.quote: The construction is generic for any linear Lie group and relies on building a matrix constructed from the Lie algebra whose kernel is spanned by a group-equivariant and permutation-invariant basis.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restrict the generic claims to connected linear groups and separately state the proved O(3) extension. Retaining arbitrary disconnected groups requires additional constraints for their component actions.
issues.overall_effect: The abstract and conclusion overstate the scope of the generic construction; arbitrary disconnected linear groups are not covered.
issues.title: The advertised arbitrary-group scope exceeds what Lie-algebra constraints determine
issues.why_classification: The supported restriction removes an explicitly advertised group regime; Lie-algebra information alone cannot recover the missing discrete symmetry constraints.

issues.failure_explanation: The paper's exact l=1 example contradicts comparability of the numbers themselves. For bl=(1,...,1), L=0, and even N, the GE-PI dimension is 1 while the PI dimension is binomial(N+2,2), which grows quadratically. For odd N the GE-PI dimension is zero. Thus the ratio does not stay bounded, and enforcing rotations can yield an increasing asymptotic reduction.

failure_location.quote: We also show that for large values of $\Nat$, the number of rotation-equivariant and permutation-invariant basis functions is of a comparable order as the number of permutation-invariant basis functions, while pre-asymptotically, a large gain can be achieved by explicitly enforcing rotation-equivariance on top of permutation-invariance.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace comparability of dimensions by precise ratio or growth-scale statements for specified parameter families, explicitly acknowledging the unbounded additional reduction from rotation equivariance.
issues.overall_effect: The advertised asymptotic comparability and the interpretation that the dimensions become increasingly close are unreliable.
issues.title: PI and GE-PI dimensions need not have comparable asymptotic order
issues.why_classification: The stated qualitative asymptotic conclusion fails in an explicitly treated nondegenerate family and must be withdrawn or replaced by a materially weaker comparison.

issues.failure_explanation: The identification of the equivariant-function dimension with the number of irreducible copies requires End_G(V^L)=K, which need not hold for real irreducible representations. For the real two-dimensional rotation representation of SO(2), both I and the quarter-turn J commute with the action. With one copy as input, the equivariant space has dimension 2, and each of its two component spaces is the entire input space, so their sum is not direct. Likewise the stated two-factor recursive dimension formula gives 8 instead of 2 for the trivial output from two such inputs.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Therefore, the complexity of obtaining the kernel of $\Mup$, using a back-substitution approach, is bounded by

issues.failure_explanation: Consider one block with l=2, N=5, L=3. The terminal raising matrix has 8 rows and 9 columns. Every column has at least two nonzero entries: a column with only one raisable occupied weight p would require a(2-p)=7 with 1≤a≤5 and 1≤2-p≤4, which is impossible. Consequently no row/column ordering can make this matrix upper triangular or trapezoidal, whose first nonzero pivot column must have only one nonzero entry. Back-substitution therefore requires an additional factorization whose cost and fill-in are not counted.
